svg.title: Big-O Notation
svg.desc: Big-O Notation. How an algorithm's cost grows with its input: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) and O(n²) side by side as n grows. Step 1, Count steps, not seconds: Reading a[5] takes 1 step at any n; a scan for a missing value takes n steps: 8, then 16. Step 2, Halving: O(log n): Discarding half the sorted range each step takes 16 cells to 1 in 4 halvings; n = 32 needs just 5. Step 3, n log n and n²: Merge-sort levels fill 4 rows of 16 (64 steps); nested loops fill the whole 16 × 16 grid (256). Step 4, What it means at scale: At n = 1,000,000 and 10⁹ steps a second: O(n) takes 1 ms, O(n log n) 20 ms, O(n²) about 17 min.

g.text: Reading a[5] takes 1 step at any n; a scan for a missing value takes n steps: 8, then 16.
Discarding half the sorted range each step takes 16 cells to 1 in 4 halvings; n = 32 needs just 5.
Merge-sort levels fill 4 rows of 16 (64 steps); nested loops fill the whole 16 × 16 grid (256).
At n = 1,000,000 and 10⁹ steps a second: O(n) takes 1 ms, O(n log n) 20 ms, O(n²) about 17 min.
time at an illustrative 10⁹ simple steps per second
Keep the fastest-growing term: n² + n is O(n²)
Log base does not matter: log₁₀ n ≈ 0.3 log₂ n
